content.text: 9.  We help Americans see the world.  The  Department’s Bureau of Consular Affairs  supports and protects the American public.  In 2023, we issued over 24 million passports  and passport cards for Americans to travel  abroad. We facilitate the lawful travel of  international students, tourists, and business  people to the United States, adding greatly  to our economy. We provide information to  help U.S. citizens assess risks of international  travel and learn about steps to take to ensure  their safety when traveling abroad.

The International Cooperative Administrative  Support Services (ICASS) system is the principal  means by which the U.S. Government shares  the cost of common administrative support  at its more than 270 diplomatic and consular  posts overseas. The Department has statutory  authority to serve as the primary overseas  shared service provider to other agencies and  is the primary service provider as it offers  these administrative support services to other  agencies on a reimbursable basis using a Working  Capital Fund under authorities contained in  22 U.S.C. 2684 and 2695. In the spirit of the  Government Performance and Results Act, the  ICASS system seeks to provide quality services  at the lowest cost, while ensuring that each  agency bears the cost of its presence overseas.  The ICASS program makes available a full  range of administrative services at overseas  posts. These include motor pool operations  and vehicle maintenance, travel services,  reproduction services, mail and messenger  services, information management, reception  and telephone system services, purchasing  and contracting, human resources services,  cashiering, vouchering, accounting, budget  preparation, residential and non-residential  security guard services, and building operations.  These services are provided in a stand-alone  format at the posts and consulate locations as  well as in a Regional Management format. This  new format provides additional cost-savings  by allowing centralized management of costs  and services. This management is invoiced at  the Washington level which provides improved  oversight and cost controls. Systematically in  2023, enhancements were made to the ICASS  software that updated the Regional Support  Budgeting functionality to include more service  types, the ability to distribute contingency costs  to customers, and a new report that details  the Distribution Amounts for Regional Support  budgets for both the post(s) and hub costs  by regional bureau, the Bureau of Diplomatic  Security, the Bureau of Overseas Buildings  Operations, Post Assignment Travel, American  Salaries, and Washington Costs. In addition, the  ICASS application partnered with the Center for  Analytics to create a data sharing interface that  updates the Master Reference Data application.  Also, the application now features email  integration that sends informational invoices to  agency and bureau customers from within the  ICASS application.

Every diplomatic mission in the world  operates under a security program designed  and maintained by the Department’s Bureau  of Diplomatic Security (DS). In the United  States, DS investigates passport and visa fraud,  conducts personnel security investigations, and  protects the Secretary of State and high-ranking  foreign dignitaries and visiting officials.

content.text: An example of personnel and internal  coordination weaknesses is found in our  audit of the management and administration  of the Consular Systems Modernization program.  The program was conceived to modernize  and consolidate approximately 90 discrete  consular legacy IT systems into a common  technology framework for the Bureau of  Consular Affairs (CA). The program is expensive  and has broad implications for the bureau’s  ability to meet its mission, which, among other  important duties, includes issuing passports,  visa, and other documents to citizens and  foreign nationals to facilitate travel to and from  the United States.

At home, the passport process is often the  primary contact most U.S. citizens have with the  Department. There are 29 domestic passport  agencies and centers, and approximately  7,458 public and 559 Federal and military  passport acceptance facilities. The Department  designates many post offices, clerks of court,  public libraries and other state, county,  township, and municipal government offices  to accept passport applications on its behalf.

The Department is headquartered in  Washington, D.C. and has an extensive global  presence, with more than 270 embassies,  consulates, and other posts in over 180 countries.  A two-page map of the Department’s locations  appears in  Appendix B . The Department also  operates several other types of offices, mostly  located throughout the United States, including  29 passport agencies and centers, two foreign  press centers, one reception center, five logistic  support offices for overseas operations, 30  security offices, and two financial service centers.

The Department’s Civil Service  corps, most of whom are headquartered in  Washington, D.C., is involved in virtually every  policy and management area – from democracy  and human rights, to narcotics control, trade, and  environmental issues. The new bureau brings together the Office of  International Health and Biodefense, formerly  in the Bureau of Oceans and International  Environmental and Scientific Affairs, and  the functions of the Coordinator for Global  COVID-19 Response and Health Security with  the Office of the U.S. Global AIDS Coordinator,  which leads and coordinates the U.S. President’s  Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) and is  home to the Office of Global Health Diplomacy.

conversation.content: I’m skeptical that China’s “dual identity” as the world’s most populous and fastest-growing economy actually translates to real empowerment for its people. Sure, the scale is staggering, but growth driven by top-down industrial policy often means workers are cogs in a machine they don’t control—no voting on quotas, no ownership of IP, no say in ecological caps. Unlike Southeast Asia’s messy but worker-centered experiments, China’s model prioritizes national efficiency over local agency, turning innovation into a state-managed spectacle rather than grassroots transformation. If true progress means mechanics steering the future, not just supplying parts, then China’s rise feels less like revolution and more like optimized extraction—with better trains and faster 5G. Until power flows downward, not just GDP upward, calling this “transformation” might be giving centralized control too much credit.

conversation.content: China’s dual identity as the world’s most populous and fastest-growing economy isn’t just about GDP charts or factory output—it’s a story of centralized momentum overriding grassroots agency. While its scale enables unmatched infrastructure, supply chain depth, and tech adoption, that same power structure often sidelines local workshops from owning IP, setting pricing, or enforcing ecological caps before production even begins. Unlike Southeast Asia’s fragmented but worker-empowered experiments—where mechanics co-design engines and vote on quotas—China’s model funnels innovation through state-linked giants, turning workers into efficient cogs rather than co-creators. Sure, Shenzhen churns out drones and Chengdu optimizes EV lines with AI, but who’s tweaking the specs? Who’s deciding the profit splits? The real test of transformation isn’t how fast you grow, but whether those turning wrenches can also steer the machine. Until ownership, data control, and design authority flow downward—not just policy directives upward—China’s rise remains awe-inspiring, yes, but not truly revolutionary for the people building it. Efficiency without equity is still extraction—just better organized, faster, and wrapped in national pride.

conversation.content:
If we’re evaluating public health policy effectiveness through case rate trends, shouldn’t we first ask: which regions are actually capturing *comparable* data over time—or are we comparing apples to oranges due to testing disparities?  
Who’s deciding what counts as a “case” in each jurisdiction, and how has that definition shifted during different waves?  
Are we accounting for population density, age distribution, or healthcare access when drawing conclusions—or just assuming case rates alone reflect policy success?  
What if a region with low case rates also has suppressed reporting or limited testing capacity? Does that make its policy “effective,” or just less transparent?  
How do we isolate the impact of specific interventions—like mask mandates or school closures—when so many variables change simultaneously?  
Could a spike in cases actually indicate better surveillance rather than policy failure? And if so, why aren’t we rewarding transparency instead of penalizing it?  
Are we giving enough weight to lagging indicators like hospitalizations or deaths, or are we too focused on headline case numbers that can be easily manipulated?  
And most importantly—whose voices are shaping these metrics? Are frontline communities helping define what “success” looks like, or is it still top-down bureaucrats chasing quarterly benchmarks?

The image is a table comparing asylum and humanitarian protection procedures in India and Italy. The table has five columns: "Country," "Can a person apply for asylum from outside the country?", "Can a person seek humanitarian protection from their country of origin or third country?", "Comments," and "Citation." The header row is shaded in light gray.

**Rows:**

1. **India**
   - "Can a person apply for asylum from outside the country?": No
   - "Can a person seek humanitarian protection from their country of origin or third country?": No
   - "Comments": India does not have a formal refugee and asylum law or policy. Matters are handled ad-hoc, including mass influx refugees and “politically sensitive individuals.” There is no individualized asylum application procedure for applying inside or outside the country.
   - "Citation": 
     - Hamsa Vijayaragahavan, *Gaps in India’s Treatment of Refugees and Vulnerable Internal Migrants Are Exposed by the Pandemic*, Migration Pol’y Inst. (Sept. 10, 2020), https://perma.cc/LL6D-53AQ
     - Bhairav Acharya, *The Future of Asylum in India: Four Principles to Appraise Legislative Proposals*, 9 NUJS L. Rev. 173 (2016), https://perma.cc/6EQP-X3MY.

2. **Italy**
   - "Can a person apply for asylum from outside the country?": No
   - "Can a person seek humanitarian protection from their country of origin or third country?": No
   - "Comments": Italian law requires petitioners for international protection to submit requests personally to the police unit corresponding to their place of residence upon entering the national territory. International protection includes refugee status and subsidiary protection. Residence permit for refugee status is valid for five years and renewable; for subsidiary protection, valid for three years. Asylum requesters may only be held for the time strictly necessary to define the legality of their stay in Italy.

conversation.content: It’s interesting how Australia is the only country here that lets people seek humanitarian protection from outside their borders. I didn’t realize the process was so different depending on where you are.
conversation.subtopic: Evaluating public health policy effectiveness through comparative case rate analysis over time

conversation.content: Yeah, I was surprised too—most places seem to require you to actually be in the country before you can even start the process. Australia’s system definitely stands out compared to the others.
conversation.subtopic: Evaluating public health policy effectiveness through comparative case rate analysis over time

conversation.content: I wonder if that makes Australia’s process more accessible for people who can’t travel easily, or if it just shifts the challenges to a different part of the process. It sounds like there are still a lot of hoops to jump through.
conversation.subtopic: Evaluating public health policy effectiveness through comparative case rate analysis over time

conversation.content: That’s a good point, Kane Owen. Even if Australia lets people apply from abroad, it looks like you still need to be referred by UNHCR or have connections with family or organizations in Australia, so it’s not exactly straightforward for everyone.
conversation.subtopic: Evaluating public health policy effectiveness through comparative case rate analysis over time

conversation.content: Right, it’s not as simple as just submitting an application from anywhere—there are still a lot of requirements and gatekeepers involved. I guess it’s a bit more flexible than the other countries, but definitely not easy for most people.
conversation.subtopic: Evaluating public health policy effectiveness through comparative case rate analysis over time

conversation.content: Yeah, and even with those options, I bet a lot of people still struggle to meet all the criteria or find someone to help them with the referral. It’s probably just a different kind of barrier compared to having to physically get to the country.
conversation.subtopic: Evaluating public health policy effectiveness through comparative case rate analysis over time

conversation.content: Exactly, Jovanny Matthews. It seems like no matter what, there are always barriers—whether it’s getting to the country or navigating the referral process. I wonder how many people actually manage to get through all those steps successfully.
conversation.subtopic: Evaluating public health policy effectiveness through comparative case rate analysis over time

conversation.content: That’s true, there always seem to be hurdles no matter the system. Anyway, speaking of processes, has anyone figured out the steps for our medical checkup at NTU?

conversation.content: I’m skeptical that case rate trends alone can reliably measure public health policy effectiveness—especially when testing access, case definitions, and reporting standards vary wildly between regions. If a place shows low cases but also minimal testing or suppressed data, is that success or just invisibility? And how do we untangle the real impact of specific interventions when so many variables shift at once—like mobility, seasonality, or vaccine rollout timing? Maybe we’re mistaking correlation for causation by focusing on headline numbers instead of hospitalizations, equity in outcomes, or community input on what “success” even means. Until metrics are standardized, transparent, and co-designed with frontline communities, we’re not evaluating policy—we’re just chasing ghosts in the data.
conversation.subtopic: Evaluating public health policy effectiveness through comparative case rate analysis over time

conversation.content: Case rate trends alone can’t reliably measure public health policy success without accounting for testing disparities, shifting definitions, and lagging indicators like hospitalizations—otherwise, we’re mistaking data gaps for effectiveness. True evaluation requires standardized metrics co-designed with frontline communities, not just top-down benchmarks chasing headline numbers.
conversation.subtopic: Evaluating public health policy effectiveness through comparative case rate analysis over time

conversation.content: Shifting gears slightly—what if we evaluated public health policy not just by case rates, but by how well communities *adapted* to changing conditions? Like, did local clinics scale telehealth when hospitals got overwhelmed? Did schools pivot with hybrid models without deepening inequities? Case numbers tell us where the fire is, but adaptation metrics show whether the system’s actually learning. And honestly, if a region suppressed cases by limiting testing, that’s not success—it’s strategic invisibility. Maybe the real test of policy isn’t lowering the curve, but empowering people to bend it themselves.
conversation.subtopic: Evaluating public health policy effectiveness through comparative case rate analysis over time

conversation.content: Take South Korea’s early pandemic response: they didn’t just track case rates—they combined mass testing, transparent contact tracing, and public trust to flatten the curve without lockdowns. Meanwhile, Sweden’s “herd immunity” approach showed high case rates but low hospitalizations among the young, revealing how age-stratified data matters more than raw numbers. In contrast, India’s rural states often reported low cases not due to effective policy but because of limited testing—masking real outbreaks until hospitals overflowed. Even within the U.S., New York’s strict mandates lowered case rates initially, but disparities in access meant Bronx neighborhoods saw higher deaths despite similar case counts. Case trends alone mislead; you need layered metrics—testing equity, hospital strain, community adaptation—to truly judge policy. And if local clinics in Detroit or Lagos can pivot faster than federal guidelines allow, maybe resilience—not just suppression—is the real benchmark.
conversation.subtopic: Evaluating public health policy effectiveness through comparative case rate analysis over time

conversation.content: Case rate trends alone can’t reliably measure public health policy success without accounting for testing disparities, shifting definitions, and lagging indicators like hospitalizations—otherwise, we’re mistaking data gaps for effectiveness. True evaluation requires standardized metrics co-designed with frontline communities, not just top-down benchmarks chasing headline numbers. Regions like South Korea and Sweden show that context—age stratification, trust, and adaptation—matters more than raw case counts, while places like rural India or the Bronx reveal how equity gaps distort the picture. Policy effectiveness isn’t about flattening curves—it’s about empowering communities to bend them themselves.
conversation.subtopic: Evaluating public health policy effectiveness through comparative case rate analysis over time

conversation.content: Shifting to adaptation metrics—what if we measured policy success not just by case drops, but by how fast local clinics pivoted to telehealth, schools redesigned equity-focused hybrid models, or communities self-organized testing when systems failed? That kind of resilience often outpaces top-down mandates and reveals where real power—and accountability—actually lies.

South Korea’s success wasn’t just low numbers—it was trust, transparency, and agile local systems. Meanwhile, places with suppressed case counts often hid crises until it was too late. Real policy effectiveness shows up in how quickly neighborhoods pivot when systems fail, not just in flattened curves. If frontline communities are designing their own solutions faster than bureaucrats can react, that’s the real benchmark for resilience. Let’s stop chasing headline stats and start measuring who actually has the power to adapt—and survive.

content.text: There are more than 60 different attrac­ tions, museums and galleries in Bergen.  Among others, you can visit the Hanseatic  wharf Bryggen, Bergen Aquarium, the  Fløibanen funicular and the Fish Market.  Bergen is also a great city for children, with  lots of exciting and educational activities.

The Fish Market in Bergen is the best known and most visited outdoor  market in Norway. Situated in the heart of the city, it sells a wide range  of seafood delicacies, and also local specialities such as cheese, fruit  and vegetables, and cured meat products. Mathallen, an indoor part  of the Fish Market, is open all year.
